zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical checkpoint: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510; supplied page subset consulted after independent scan reading. The scan remains authoritative. Source: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: CC BY 4.0, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ .

lines.note: Nemonogatari is conversation while lying down; the Portuguese gloss explicitly supplies the reclining posture.
Nemui expresses being sleepy, literally glossed as having sleep; the following two indented forms belong to the same adjective family.
Nemusa is the corresponding noun for sleepiness. The long s is visible; no independent Portuguese gloss is printed on this row.
Nemǔ is the contracted adverbial form of nemui. The downward-pointing mark is retained as a caron, not silently replaced with a circumflex.

runs.text: Hũa raiz de Cazzura com que

lines.note: Nemurasaki is described as a root of a climbing plant used for dyeing; Cazzura is a Japanese plant term embedded in the Portuguese explanation, not an additional headword.
The root dyes material purple. This short Portuguese continuation completes the botanical entry without warranting a modern species identification.
Nemuri denotes sleep; nemuri wo samasu means waking or dispelling sleep. The paragraph sign introduces the example rather than a separate entry.
The gloss means awakening from sleep. Yoru hiru begins an example about remaining awake by night and day.
Samashite completes the waking construction, and yōjin kibishiki describes strict vigilance. The final kikoye keru is a reported or narrative expression, not a malformed modern verb.
The upright Taif. label identifies the cited source; Lib. 26 belongs to the italic apparatus. The translation begins with being awake during the day.

runs.text: & de noite parece que tinhão grande vigia.

lines.note: The translation continues with night and says that they apparently maintained great vigilance, matching the preceding Japanese example.
The principal forms identify nemuru, here glossed as sleeping lightly or dozing. The printed toſ- continues into quenejar below.
Quenejar completes the Portuguese verb toſquenejar, to doze; this is a genuine continuation row rather than a new dictionary item.

Nemuri-i describes sleeping while seated or leaning. The scan has continuous dormindo and a visible gap before the final j of Nemuri j; the supplied NINJAL headword checkpoint independently records that gap. The divided aßenta- continues below.
The gloss completes seated or lightly leaning sleep. Mina yeye- begins the description of everyone being like drunken people; the divided historical yeyer(u) should not be modernized.

runs.text: ru monono gotocuni natte cǒbeuo vna-

lines.note: The scan supports gotocuni, corresponding to gotoku ni, rather than OCR gorocuni. The example describes becoming like drunken people and lowering the head; cǒbe retains the printed caron.
Tarete completes unatarete, with heads bowed, followed by the state of sleeping. The source is Taif., book 24; the final stop after the number is visible.

runs.text: Eſtauão dormindo todos com a cabeça inclinada

lines.note: The Portuguese says that all were sleeping with their heads inclined, translating the posture in the preceding Japanese lines.
The comparison with drunken people completes the translation and confirms the function of yeye-ru monono gotocuni above.
Nemushiro is a sleeping mat; the brief Portuguese definition is complete on this physical row.
Nen is explained by toshi, years, and is said to occur in compounds. The line-end compoſ- belongs to Portuguese composto below.
The example nannen asks how many years. The Portuguese question confirms the interrogative reading rather than a personal name.
Sunen denotes many or several years. The scan includes a paragraph sign before the example which the OCR omitted.
This homographic nen means thought or attention, not years. Nen wo iruru and the following divided tsukau describe applying care or diligence.
Cǒ completes tçucǒ, the alternative expression for applying attention. The next example starts with upright Nẽ-, whose abbreviation tilde belongs to the Japanese text, not an isolated italic vowel.
Nen wo chirasu is scattering one's thoughts or thinking of various things. The Portuguese derra- continues across the physical row boundary.
Mar completes derramar, here figuratively dispersing thought. This continuation closes the second example under nen, thought.
Nenaori is turning over while asleep. The principal forms are retained as printed rather than being expanded or rewritten in modern Japanese.
The other flank completes the description of turning onto one's other side in sleep.
Nenashi kazura is identified as a kind of climbing plant, literally glossed here as a kind of ivy. The printed era is retained rather than replaced by a modern botanical name.

runs.text: Seta ſem cabeça nem ferro. ¶ Per

lines.note: Nenashiya is an arrow without a head or iron tip. Per introduces the metaphorical use explained by the following lines.
Met. completes the usage label. Nenashiya wo motte mairu means bringing such an arrow or, in the gloss's figurative extension, a weapon intended only to hurt.

runs.text: arma pera ferir, ou fazer pouco mal, & não

lines.note: The weapon is for wounding or doing little harm. The final negative carries over to the contrast with killing on the next row.
Not for killing completes the contrast and the metaphorical explanation; this short line is not detached furniture.
Nenbut represents the Buddhist invocation nembutsu, paraphrased as invoking or calling upon the Buddha. The final bare t is retained without expansion to tçu.
The Portuguese continuation names Fotoque as the being invoked. Fotoque is a Japanese term embedded in Portuguese and is flagged for whole-word typeface review.

runs.text: Nencǒ. Cǒuo fineru. i, Fotoqeno mayeni

lines.note: Nencǒ is explained as handling incense and burning it before the Buddha. The printed carons in the headword and Cǒuo are retained independently of later spelling conventions.
Kō wo taku is burning incense. The scan has perfumes with f, not OCR perſumes. Fotoque is a Japanese term within the Portuguese explanation and remains flagged for whole-word typeface review.
Nendai is years, age, or a period of time, with toshi and yo as the Japanese explanatory words.
Nendai ikahodo zo asks how long or how many years. The Portuguese interrogative begins here and continues onto the next row.
The gloss completes the question about elapsed time or number of years; the printed hà is preserved rather than modernized.

runs.text: Cronica, ou liuro de historia das

lines.note: Nendaiki is a chronicle or historical record. The initial letter of historia is the italic h, not the OCR's b.

runs.text: couſas que acontecem em cada era, que em Ia

lines.note: The chronicle records events in each era. The word Iapão is physically divided after Ia without adding an inferred hyphen.

runs.text: pão ſe varia à võtade dos q̃ gouernão a Tẽca.

lines.note: The dictionary says that eras in Japan change at the will of those governing the realm. Tẽca is the embedded Japanese term tenka; the contraction and printed accents remain literal.

runs.text: Molher como ama, que cria, & traz

lines.note: Nene is a woman acting as a nurse or caregiver. The scan reads Molher, not OCR Molhar, and the following row explains her care of the child.
Carrying the child habitually in her arms completes the caregiver definition. The final upright X. is the regional usage label, not part of the Portuguese sentence.
Nengiū means throughout or within the year, clarified by toshi no uchi. The scan supports Toxinovchi rather than OCR Toxmnovchi; the definition continues at the top of column 2.

This completes the year-long sense from column 1. The example says that the speaker spent the year ill; yamicuraita uses the historical -aita ending, and the scan ends it with a stop rather than a hyphen.
The Portuguese translates the example as having spent this entire year sick, confirming the temporal sense of nengiū.

runs.text: Era, nome geral das Eras que em

lines.note: Nengō is an era designation. The second noun reads Eras, not OCR Etas; the sentence continues with the practice in Japan.
The gloss says that Japanese era names change repeatedly. This is the dictionary's historical description, not an assertion about a present-day schedule.
Nengoro denotes affectionate attention or caresses. The Portuguese agaſalhado is retained as the printed historical noun.
Nengorona describes a person who gives much affectionate attention. The italic peßoa and the abbreviated relative q̃ belong to the Portuguese definition.

runs.text: ou caricias, ou couſa de amor, & agaſalhado.

lines.note: The definition continues with caresses and matters of love or affectionate treatment, rather than introducing another Japanese form.
Nengoroni is the adverb, translated as lovingly and with affectionate attention. Adu. is the grammatical label.
The affectionate sense is completed, then Item introduces a second sense, minutely or exactly. The terminal e- continues on the next row.
Xactamente completes exactamente, the careful or exact manner associated with nengoroni.

runs.text: Nengu. i, Chiguiǒ yori mainen aguru mo-

lines.note: Nengu is annual dues, explained as what is submitted each year from a holding. The final mo- continues the Japanese noun mono below.

runs.text: Rendimento, ou foro de cada anno,

lines.note: Mono completes the Japanese explanation. The Portuguese defines yearly revenue or dues; two n types are visible in anno rather than the OCR's ano.
The revenue is offered to the lord. The printed cedilla in ofereçe is preserved, not regularized to modern spelling.

runs.text: Deſejo que hum tem no cora-

lines.note: Nenguan is a desire held in the heart. The final cora- is continued by ção on the following row.
Nennenno nenguan nari is a long-standing desire, held over many years. He begins the Portuguese translation after the complete Japanese example.
The translation finishes as a desire of many years, matching the repeated-year expression rather than adding a separate headword.
Nenget is years and months, paraphrased by toshi and tsuki. The final bare t is retained as a historical checked coda.
Nenget wo heru means passing through years and months. The object particle is attached to the checked-final noun in the printed romanization.
Months completes the Portuguese pair years and months; the physical continuation row remains distinct.

Nengyōji is the duty or officer conducting the year's affairs. The mark after yacu is read as a damaged terminal stop with abrasion above it, not the OCR's extra a; its exact punctuation shape remains a minor caveat.
The Portuguese defines an officer for one year and directs the reader to Guiǒji. That cross-reference is a Japanese term within Portuguese editorial prose.

Nenja is glossed as the active partner in the act that the missionary dictionary condemns as an unspeakable sin. This reports the source's historical terminology; nefando is one continuous printed word, not ne fando.
The principal forms of nenjiru/nenzuru are glossed as thinking or meditating. The distinction from the preceding sexual-role noun is supplied by both morphology and Portuguese.
Nenjo concerns the passing of years. The repeated example reads Nenjouo with e, not OCR Nonjouo, and furu expresses spending or passing time.

runs.text: Ler, ou rezar com deuação por algũ

lines.note: This nenju means reading or reciting devotionally from a book. The Portuguese definition continues with the object liuro on the next row.
The book completes the gloss. Nenju suru exemplifies the verbal use, and Idem refers back to the same devotional reading or recitation.
The second nenju is prayer beads, paraphrased as thinking or devotional beads. The source's gentios is retained as historical missionary language, not adopted as a present-day characterization.

runs.text: Nenju uo teni curu l, Nenju uo tçu-

lines.note: The two examples describe turning the beads in one's hand or fingering them. The second verb is divided as tçu- plus maguru on the next row.
Maguru completes the verb for fingering the beads. The Portuguese explains praying with the beads rather than reading a book, distinguishing the two nenju entries.
Nenmō is wishing or desire, explained by omoi and nozomu. The abbreviated Nẽ begins the example in upright Japanese type; no line-end hyphen is supplied where none is established.
The divided nenmō wo toguru means fulfilling a wish. The Portuguese Comprir is retained as printed rather than modernized to cumprir.
Nennai means within this year, with toshi no uchi as its Japanese explanation. The word space before vchi is visible here, unlike the closed spelling in column 1.
This nen nen means every year, equated with toshidoshi or mainen. The Portuguese anno has two n types; the separate homograph for thoughts follows below.
All the years completes the distributive yearly gloss. The repeated annos belongs to the translation, not another Japanese example.
The other nen nen denotes thoughts or each individual thought. The repeated spelling is retained because the Portuguese distinguishes its meaning from every year.
Nenobi here is stretching oneself while lying down. The unusual printed eſpriguiçar is retained rather than supplied with a modernizing vowel.

runs.text: Ceremonia, ou feſta que ſe faz pollo

lines.note: The second nenobi names a ceremony or festival. The scan reads pollo with its first o present, not OCR pllo; the following rows describe the New Year pine custom.

runs.text: Xǒguachi cõ pinheiro q̃ ſe arrãca com a raiz,

lines.note: The rite occurs at Shōgatsu and uses a pine pulled up with its root. Xǒguachi is a Japanese term inside the Portuguese sentence; its entire word is kept together typographically rather than split after Xǒ.

runs.text: & ſe mete dentro em caſa com deſejo de vi-

lines.note: The uprooted pine is brought into the house with a wish to live long. The final vi- continues the Portuguese viver below.

runs.text: uer muitos annos, como o pinheiro que dura

lines.note: The desired long life is compared with the pine's longevity. This explains the symbolism within the source rather than requiring a botanical claim from the reviewer.
The pine's endurance closes the explanation. Nenobi no matsu then names the pine used in the ceremony, with its Portuguese gloss divided at ſo-.

runs.text: bre que ſe faz esta ceremonia, & feſta.

lines.note: Bre completes sobre: the ceremony and festival are performed with reference to this pine. The continuation is still part of the nenobi entry.
Nenpo is glossed as the beginning of the year, paraphrased by toshi no hajime. The printed headword is retained without normalization to another New Year term.
The example is a formal New Year congratulation. Medetaku soro supplies the congratulatory formula; the Portuguese begins Dou, I give.
The Portuguese completes a wish for a good new year. The final upright S. marks written usage, separate from the italic gloss.
Nenki is a stated quantity or term of years. The repeated example begins Nẽ- with a visible tilde over e, not the OCR's õ.

Nenki wo sadamuru means fixing a term of years; the scan supports m in ſadamuru. The alternative is read as ſaſu, whose first long-s head is worn and remains a minor caveat. The Portuguese an- continues as nos on the next page; the separate bottom nos, is its catchword.

zones.label: Column 2 catchword
zones.note: The catchword repeats the opening nos, of the following page.
